items.title: 30.6 Determining the Possible Structure of a Molecule from 1H NMR

source_refs.note: Topic 30.6 with Example 30.2 (PDF 211); the spectrum is redrawn as a sketch. The printed 'No. of peaks = No of protons' and the 3.9 ppm 'doublet' are corrected in warnings.

blocks.text: The structure of an unknown compound can be deduced from its 1H NMR spectrum by putting the information together like a puzzle.

items: Count the peaks: the number of peaks is the number of proton environments.
Use the chemical shift of each peak to identify functional groups (Table 30.1).
Use the peak areas to find the number of hydrogen atoms in each environment.
Analyse the splitting: number of sub-peaks = n + 1, so n (adjacent protons) = number of sub-peaks - 1.
Combine the information to assemble the structure.

blocks.alt: 1H NMR spectrum of the ester in Example 30.2: absorption of energy against chemical shift, delta ppm, from 6 to 0. A small group of four sub-peaks labelled 2H near 3.9, a tall single peak labelled 3H near 2.1, a group of three sub-peaks labelled 3H near 1.3, and a small TMS peak at 0.
blocks.caption: Example 30.2: the 1H NMR spectrum of an ester (original drawing after the spectrum printed in Example 30.2).
Example 30.2: the 1H NMR spectrum of an ester
rows: -CH2- next to an electronegative O atom

blocks.text: Combining the three signals gives the structure CH3-CO-O-CH2-CH3, ethyl ethanoate.
